newsitem.title: USA: Forex mart sees no bite behind Japan's dollar bark.
newsitem.headline: Forex mart sees no bite behind Japan's dollar bark.

text.p: Japanese warnings of foreign exchange market intervention to curb the yen's rapid fall against the dollar were met with skepticism by currency traders and economists on Thursday.

Any active Japanese intervention would probably have to be part of a coordinated effort between the G3 nations and many market participants believe the United States and Germany are loath to spark a reversal in the greenback.
And even Japan -- U.S. trade pressure notwithstanding -- appears to have little incentive for wanting a stronger yen and a weaker dollar.
A recent decline in Japanese long-term interest rates has highlighted market pessimism about the outlook for Japan's economy, which is struggling to cope with a newly-enacted consumption tax hike.
The robust dollar has provided the Japanese with a modicum of relief at a time when domestic demand-led growth appears far off.

"I don't think Japan necessarily wants the dollar to go any higher but they do want a strong dollar because they're enjoying and benefitting from it," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp.
"They are afraid of the United States getting overly concerned about the strong dollar, but I don't think they have a great incentive to intervene."
Members of Japan's Ministry of Finance offered their most explicit warnings to date about the dollar's sharp rise against the yen on Thursday.

Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in a speech to bank executives that recent yen moves were "obviously excessive" and cautioned that any such fluctuations would be dealt with "decisively" and in "a timely manner."

Eisuke Sakakibara -- dubbed "Mr. Yen" for his past influence on the currency markets and head of the ministry's International Finance Bureau -- called recent moves in dollar/yen "too rapid" and warned that intervention was possible if foreign exchange rates deviated from fundamentals.

"I don't think the market really believes the Japanese are ready to put money in the marketplace and I especially do not feel that anybody thinks Rubin is ready to call Greenspan and ask him to sell dollars," he added. "It's just not in the cards."

Treasury Secretary Rubin said on Thursday that the U.S. shared Japan's concern on recent yen moves because of their impact on Japan's external surplus -- the first overt sign of apprehension from the administration about the dollar's rise against the yen.
